Offload, WAL and queue optimization candidates
Compare an optimization with its baseline
macOS, Linux ARM64 and Kubernetes campaigns
Compare JIT and Native AOT on a new machine
Safe storage initialization for dedicated kind faults

pageProps.contentHtml:
Application, Resource and Autoscaling Benchmarks

SlimFaas includes a reproducible native-local benchmark for the warm synchronous proxy path, asynchronous enqueue and delivery, and scale-to-zero followed by PromQL scale-out.

CPU, RAM and throughput

The application benchmarks already export these measurements. Unit tests check the collectors and report calculations with fixtures; their execution times are not performance results. Use the following fields for the website results table:

Workload Throughput CPU RAM Evidence
HTTP sync Successful requests/s, excluding warmup Aggregate runtime CPU ms/successful request Sampled peak aggregate working set, MiB results.json: LatencyRuns[].RatePerSecond and .Resources
HTTP async, paced and burst Accepted messages/s (HTTP 202), excluding delivery drain Aggregate runtime CPU ms/accepted message, including delivery drain Sampled peak aggregate working set, MiB, including drain LatencyRuns[].AsyncResources; AsyncWorkloads[].Resources and .RatePerSecond
MemoryLab Set/Get, HashSet, counters, Files and mixed Successful operations/s; Files also export logical payload MiB/s Aggregate runtime CPU ms/successful operation during load Peak of the sum of runtime nodes in each 500 ms round operations.json: report, resources, resourceWindow
Streams, Jobs, official .NET/Python WebSocket clients Acceptance/request rate and independently observed delivery/completion rates Runtime CPU during load and a separate drain resource window Peak cluster working set in each window feature-results.json: Rows, Resources, DrainResources, Receipts, Samples
Microbenchmarks BenchmarkDotNet operation timings Elapsed operation time, not process CPU consumption Managed allocated bytes/op, not process RAM BenchmarkDotNet reports

The HTTP summary.md contains a combined throughput/CPU/RAM table with repetition counts, request failures, missing deliveries and duplicates. CPU is CPU time per accepted message or successful request, not CPU utilization %. RAM is measured in MiB (bytes / 1,048,576). The runtime totals exclude the load generator, function processes, local supervisor and container/VM overhead; background consensus and diagnostics work remain included. A 500 ms HTTP or approximately 1 s platform sampling interval can miss shorter RAM spikes. Acceptance throughput must not be relabelled as delivery throughput. Keep delivery counts, latencies and drain results beside it.

Measured macOS Native AOT results

The 17–18 November 2026 campaign ran three SlimFaas Local nodes on an ARM64 Mac with .NET 11.0.100. These are selected measurements from the repaired runtime at bbcf2147. HTTP values come from the two candidate passes in the first completed ABBA block under the 20 GiB disk reserve, with two repetitions per pass. The other workloads use two repetitions per case. Full source identities, cases and comparisons are in the campaign report.

Workload Payload Concurrency Median throughput Median completions/s incl. drain Median CPU ms/op Peak RAM MiB
HTTP sync 4 KiB 16 7,605.20 req/s — 0.47 511.75
HTTP async 4 KiB 16 1,113.58 accepted/s 875.75 1.74 512.97
HTTP sync 4 MiB 16 110.74 req/s — 25.26 638.44
HTTP async 4 MiB 16 69.06 accepted/s 35.31 123.95 651.45
Set 4 KiB 16 142.55 op/s — 2.93 496.91
Get 4 KiB 16 19,815.14 op/s — 0.33 498.42
HashSet 4 KiB 16 126.61 op/s — 2.68 589.31
Increment — 16 104.34 op/s — 2.38 501.67
File upload 1 MiB 4 42.65 op/s — 29.18 386.11
File download 1 MiB 4 466.57 op/s — 5.98 361.30
File cross-node 1 MiB 4 68.29 op/s — 33.05 393.06
Streams, one subscriber 4 KiB 16 796.35 accepted/s 4.01 1.93 442.55
Jobs — 16 1,246.31 accepted/s 13.09 0.96 352.75
WebSocket .NET sync 4 KiB 16 118.68 req/s — 4.12 353.19
WebSocket .NET async 4 KiB 16 379.11 accepted/s 41.03 2.32 429.84
WebSocket Python async 4 KiB 16 945.74 accepted/s 40.80 2.38 925.06

Peak RAM is the largest sampled aggregate working set across the listed repetitions. HTTP async CPU and RAM include drain. Streams, Jobs and WebSocket acceptance CPU and RAM cover submission. The Files runs had an explicit 16 MiB work budget per warmup and load window. Their payload column gives the size of each file. These are descriptive results from this machine. The full HTTP comparison failed its non-regression criteria, with the async case at 1 MiB + 1 byte and concurrency 16 exceeding guardrails in seven of eight pair comparisons.

To regenerate the HTTP table from retained results without starting a runtime, target or benchmark, use the already built driver:

dotnet benchmarks/SlimFaas.Benchmarks/bin/Release/net11.0/SlimFaas.Benchmarks.dll report \
  --input artifacts/slimfaas-local-benchmark/overnight/results.json \
  --output artifacts/slimfaas-local-benchmark/overnight/publication-summary.md

report --input only reads JSON and writes Markdown. It does not reconstruct missing metrics or certify acceptance. It reports unavailable resource values when any repetition lacks them. The table uses mean per-repetition throughput and median per-repetition CPU/peak RAM; raw repetitions remain in results.json. Before publishing measured rows here, attach the runtime and driver source/hash, OS/architecture, compilation mode, node count, payload, concurrency, durations, repetitions and links to the raw reports and both enclosing-reference verdicts. The JSON's framework/OS describe the driver host; obtain the measured product's compilation mode and source from its manifest. Keep macOS Native AOT and Linux managed/trimmed results separate. No final-source overnight results have been added by the 17 November reporting review.

For MemoryLab platform comparisons, rss_mib now means peak cluster sum, not largest individual node. Missing, duplicate, invalid or failed node samples make resource evidence inconclusive. The sampler reads the live process_working_set_bytes collector instead of the five-second diagnostics gauge. Historical per-node-maximum verdicts must not be presented as cluster RAM acceptance; retain their originals and qualify any offline recalculation. Use the platform comparison for this cluster measure; MemoryLab's separate report command remains a per-node slope/cooldown diagnostic. Legacy CPU totals for MemoryLab can be calculated from the live process_cpu_seconds_total boundary deltas only when every node has both boundaries, unchanged process_start_time_seconds and nondecreasing counters. Missing evidence is unavailable, not zero CPU.

Complete feature campaign and offline export

The default .bin/run-platform-matrix.py blocks now include data and features, in addition to the existing HTTP and MemoryLab set/mixed controls. The same frozen C# driver generates work in every ABBA role. Python controls platforms and receiver processes; it does not generate the timed feature load. Build the drivers and both reference/candidate products before measurements. Container images must contain the same updated benchmark tools, official SDKs and fixture sources; an old image with a new launcher is not a compatible driver.

Block Cases Integrity and timing
http Direct/sync/async; steady, paced, burst; existing payload/concurrency matrix IDs, delivery, duplicates, queue drain; acceptance and completion windows are separate
data slimdata-set, get, set, delete, hashset, hashget, hashdelete, increment, decrement Isolated operations; reads/deletes preseed outside load; final values checked on every node. Set reads use the consistent API; hashset reads retain their documented visibility semantics
data files-upload, files-download, files, files-unique Upload only, preseeded download only, cross-node upload/read cycle, bounded unique uploads. Changing overwrite contents, length and SHA-256 verification, all-node final validation
features Streams with one/two functions 200 accepted messages, independent per-function receipts, missing/duplicate/corrupt checks and committed ACK/lag drain
features Jobs 200 real jobs, independent started/completed receipts and Succeeded state on every node; request latency and submission-to-start samples
features .NET and Python WebSocket sync, async, events Official SDK receivers; full response SHA-256, first-byte timing, callback receipts and two-function event fan-out

New cases use concurrency 1/4/16 and three repetitions by default. Files and WebSocket use the HTTP payload list. Isolated data cases have an unmeasured warmup. Reads are preseeded and verified before collection. Delete cases stop when each seeded key has been deleted once; unique file uploads are bounded to 200 operations. After successful all-node validation, the data block deletes only its own file IDs through the public API, outside measurement. Failed data, WALs, journals and raw results remain available. Direct MemoryLab invocations retain files unless --cleanup-owned-files true is supplied. Files report logical payload MiB/s, not the sum of upload and download network traffic. Runtime RSS excludes the generator's payload buffers. In the direct HTTP control, runtime CPU/RAM represent idle cluster background work, not the target function. Mixed workload CPU/RAM describe the whole mix, never each constituent operation. Jobs keep a configured dispatch limit of 16 in this feature profile; request concurrency and job dispatch parallelism are different settings.

Receiver receipt polling and queue/job state confirmation are included in the observed completion window, so completion rates are conservative and distinct from acceptance rates. DrainSeconds records the additional observation time. For WebSocket async workloads, successful receiver receipts and refreshed all-node queue totals verify drain on the isolated benchmark cluster. Virtual functions do not publish the per-function depth gauges used by the HTTP benchmark. The Jobs profile launches real processes/pods; it measures their lifecycle, including startup. It does not claim isolated scheduler capacity. Keep cold start, timeout, cancellation, retries, reconnect and recovery tests in the existing reliability campaigns rather than mixing faults into healthy capacity.

The shared benchmarks/Common/ClusterResourceMonitor.cs collector takes explicit initial/final samples and periodic 500 ms samples. Every node must have live CPU, RSS and an unchanged process start identity. Counter resets, missing nodes and invalid samples cannot become zero usage. Async Raft diagnostics additionally wait for a refresh on every node; the final refresh wait is outside the live CPU window. MemoryLab's older memory.csv remains available for historical adapters.

Launch a prepared configuration manually when the machine is idle:

python3 .bin/run-platform-matrix.py \
  --config artifacts/pr506/your-frozen-platform-config.json \
  --output artifacts/pr506/your-new-feature-campaign

# Resume completed phases with exactly the same sources, binaries and settings.
python3 .bin/run-platform-matrix.py \
  --config artifacts/pr506/your-frozen-platform-config.json \
  --output artifacts/pr506/your-new-feature-campaign --resume

There is no overall campaign duration limit. The full feature matrix can take more than one night; use --blocks data or --blocks features for separate, fresh campaigns. Individual requests/drains remain bounded. Kubernetes phases have a configurable phase_timeout_seconds (default seven days). Disk guards stop new cases below 20 GiB free. Completed attempts and failures are retained. For capacity measurements on a space-constrained host, set workload_args to include --no-http-journal or --no-data-journal. These options retain compressed HTTP latency samples or data operation samples, resource data and integrity checks. Use the detailed journals for transport reconciliation. Keep the same journal setting in each comparison role. Use --file-work-budget-mib to cap the logical payload in each warmup and measured file case. Its value must fit one payload per worker. A capped test may complete before its duration limit. Use --feature-scenarios jobs ws or --data-scenarios files files-download to run selected cases in a fresh output directory. A partially executed phase without execution.json is deliberately not restarted in place: inspect and stop its owned processes, retain its directory, then use a fresh campaign. Never attach to an unverified saved PID or change a WAL marker.

campaign-identity.json freezes configuration, selected blocks, launcher hashes and local executable/managed dependency hashes. Resume refuses changes or a legacy campaign without this identity. Immutable image digests are required for container configurations. Comparisons also verify matching driver assemblies and fixture hashes before accepting evidence. The same output directory cannot be used for a new candidate. A known candidate integrity failure remains FAIL even if its reference has missing measurements or a later repeat passes. Incomplete measurements remain INCONCLUSIVE. New feature performance is OBSERVED, not a non-regression PASS: retain the established HTTP/MemoryLab budgets and calibrate new budgets before asserting optimization gains.

Generate publication artifacts without launching any workload:

dotnet benchmarks/SlimFaas.Benchmarks/bin/Release/net11.0/SlimFaas.Benchmarks.dll report \
  --campaign artifacts/pr506/your-new-feature-campaign \
  --output artifacts/pr506/your-new-feature-campaign/publication.md

This writes versioned publication.json, publication.csv and publication.md. It adapts HTTP, MemoryLab, feature and supported historical standalone reports; raw files are never rewritten. Every repetition keeps units, payload, concurrency, latency, CPU, peak RAM, integrity, window and raw source links. JSON summaries retain minimum/median/maximum per experiment, with unavailable values when any repetition lacks evidence. Source SHA-256 and nearby parameters.json preserve product/driver/environment attribution. Different experiments, SDKs, platforms and measurement windows are not pooled. Missing repetitions, unsupported legacy shapes and failed executions remain visible. Review these artifacts before explicitly adding measured rows to this page.

Offload, WAL and queue optimization candidates

Use 1 MiB (1,048,576 bytes) as the general async body offload threshold. Bodies larger than the threshold use Files. WAL directories created by SlimData on Windows use 64 KiB. New Linux and macOS WALs use the host page size. Preserve the stored geometry when reopening an existing WAL.

In the independent macOS repeat, a 512 KiB threshold increased completed throughput for 1 MiB bodies at concurrency 16 from about 12 to 190–199 messages/s. CPU fell from 124–127 to 22–23 ms per accepted message, and sampled peak RAM fell from 1,596–1,643 to 562–618 MiB. The overall threshold comparison exceeded the guardrails in all eight reference–candidate pairs, including async bursts. The comparison of fresh 64 KiB WALs with the 16 KiB macOS default also exceeded at least one guardrail in every pair of both campaigns. Keep the defaults above. See the initial campaign and repeat for the full case tables and interrupted attempts.

In both campaigns, Jobs, Streams and WebSocket recorded all 16,000 expected receipts and no missing, duplicate or corrupt receipts. The code comparison exceeded HTTP non-regression guardrails. MemoryLab passed Set and mixed at concurrency 48 in both campaigns. At concurrency 12, the Set throughput failure recurred and the mixed workload passed only in the repeat.

Prepare independent tuning configurations without running them:

python3 .bin/prepare-platform-tuning.py \
  --config artifacts/pr506/your-frozen-platform-config.json \
  --output artifacts/pr506/tuning-profiles

The generator creates nine configurations, including reference controls: WAL 4/8/16/32/64 KiB and thresholds 128/256/512 KiB/1 MiB. Every configuration uses the same product for A and B, changes only one setting, and includes payloads one byte below, exactly at, and one byte above each threshold, alongside the configured HTTP controls (including 2/4 MiB by default). Existing duration, warmup and concurrency arguments are retained. Fresh volumes are mandatory. Local/Podman preparation refuses existing WAL directories; Kubernetes initialization refuses incompatible or unmarked existing WALs. These settings are benchmark fixtures, not a new production migration mechanism.

QueuePipelineBenchmarks prepares current ZLinq, .NET LINQ and direct-loop variants for running/retry selection, with empty/200/2000-element queues and semantic equivalence tests. Routing microbenchmarks remain the control. No benchmark was run while implementing these variants. Adopt a runtime variant only after repeated ABBA comparisons beat both enclosing references beyond observed variation and preserve throughput, latency, CPU, RAM and integrity budgets. Keep serialization, copy elimination and file I/O experiments separate.

The implementation handoff records the isolated candidate branches, validation and remaining manual runs.

The 17 November PR #506 handoff records the merge assessment, CPU/RAM evidence and follow-up scope. The repository benchmark skill describes how to check current ownership before resuming and attribute results to the measured runtime revision.

The completed .NET 11 campaign report retains macOS Native AOT and Podman/Kubernetes managed ARM64 comparisons, failed guardrails, incomplete HTTP references and a Kubernetes duplicate-delivery failure. Its performance summary and file-index metadata identify the frozen sources, outputs and separate maintenance/isolation segments. The completed campaigns do not establish non-regression or LTS certification.

The 16 November final-source endurances complete all six Native macOS/managed kind roles, with 92,332 confirmed operations, 35,186 separate unknown outcomes and zero confirmed loss or receipt corruption. One extra successful delivery on an unknown outcome during an injected fault remains counted. Those recovery/integrity results do not replace the still-required formal performance comparisons or establish LTS acceptance. The final-source managed microbenchmark ABBA retains 296 valid case executions, including routing/allocation gains and seven consistently slower cases above 110% of reference time. These descriptive microbenchmarks remain separate from application non-regression acceptance.

The 15 November follow-up retains bounded Kubernetes reproductions, managed-OOM audits, failed healthy-delivery controls and separate allocation regressions. Its corrections preserve wire formats, queue deadlines and WAL geometry defaults. These diagnostic passes do not replace the formal matrices; each runtime revision requires its own final validation.

The opt-in Files acceptance policy uses SlimData__Files__RequiredDurableCopies: 0 retains historical acceptance, 1 confirms local persistence, and 2 requires a distinct confirmed persisted remote copy before atomic publication. Compare these policies at fixed WAL geometry and offload threshold before combining improvements. Record acceptance and first-delivery distributions, confirmed/unknown IDs, duplicate receipts, process CPU/allocations/GC/RSS, WAL/Files I/O and inter-node traffic with their exact sampling windows. Periodic reference repair and directory synchronization are part of the runtime cost; kernel I/O counters do not separately identify WAL and Files writes. The underlying command envelope remains unchanged, but atomic admission adds SLDC/6: use separate clusters for an SLDC/5 reference and SLDC/6 candidate. Upgrade every member of a candidate cluster together. The dedicated live admission-fault matrix and final-source performance verdict remain pending.

The source511 application report records passing targeted volume faults and refusal/cleanup without a remote copy. Its bounded cost screen uses 0–1–2–2–1–0 with both surrounding references, then one complete repeat after contradictory checks. It remains inconclusive; the two-copy budget failures are retained. CPU to first confirmed drain and CPU through the full idle/cleanup observation are separate scopes. A short batch does not replace timed HTTP/MemoryLab comparisons. Subsequent pooled verification microprobes and component tests require their own application validation. The subsequent admission initialization investigation retains an HTTP 500 in the first source511 reference. An incomplete or unhealthy reference cannot establish non-regression; its original state and per-ID accounting remain preserved while the reproduced serializer defect is corrected. The corrected-source follow-up passes all four enclosing-reference comparisons for the bounded two-copy 200 × 1 MiB/C16 case. This diagnostic result does not replace the full timed HTTP/MemoryLab matrices or earlier policy-cost failures.

Run the benchmark

One managed driver, benchmarks/SlimFaas.Benchmarks, provides micro, target, run, compare and the offline report command:

dotnet build benchmarks/SlimFaas.Benchmarks -c Release \
  -p:PublishAot=false -p:SelfContained=false -p:SkipClientAppBuild=true
dotnet benchmarks/SlimFaas.Benchmarks/bin/Release/net11.0/SlimFaas.Benchmarks.dll micro --list flat
dotnet benchmarks/SlimFaas.Benchmarks/bin/Release/net11.0/SlimFaas.Benchmarks.dll micro --extended --filter '*RoutingQuery*'
dotnet benchmarks/SlimFaas.Benchmarks/bin/Release/net11.0/SlimFaas.Benchmarks.dll target --port 31080
# With the runtime, target and scaling fixture already running:
dotnet benchmarks/SlimFaas.Benchmarks/bin/Release/net11.0/SlimFaas.Benchmarks.dll run --profile async-queue
dotnet benchmarks/SlimFaas.Benchmarks/bin/Release/net11.0/SlimFaas.Benchmarks.dll compare \
  --criteria non-regression --baseline before/results.json --candidate after/results.json

micro retains BenchmarkDotNet filters, exporters and --extended. Existing option-only microbenchmark invocations remain accepted. Invoking without a command returns exit code 2; help returns 0; malformed commands return 1. compare retains exit codes 0 (pass), 1 (failure) and 2 (inconclusive). The HTTP driver retains its exports, load profiles and deadlines. The scripts build this driver before measurement. Use the same frozen driver and configuration for both sides of each new application comparison. Record the driver hash separately from each runtime hash. Earlier source-pinned reports retain their original project names and binaries.

The driver runs managed code even when its targets are Native AOT executables or containerized runtimes. Build and publish the measured products separately with their own settings; the managed driver does not change their compilation mode. For a framework-dependent driver publication, use the same global PublishAot=false, SelfContained=false and SkipClientAppBuild=true properties. The platform tools image publishes a self-contained, untrimmed managed driver.

Analysis scope and ownership

The C# drivers own workload generation, application timing, exports and comparison criteria. Python coordinates environments/faults and independently reconciles receipts; shell scripts provide launch/environment adapters. Shared paths should delegate to those owners instead of introducing a second load or statistics loop.

Benchmark C# projects are excluded from Sonar with SonarQubeExclude, while the targeted script inventory supplies sonar.exclusions. Runtime, SDK, release and production tools stay eligible for analysis. Benchmark builds/tests continue in CI. Coverage exclusions alone do not exclude static analysis. The completed-scan check waits for processing, checks submitted C# project classification, rejects indexed benchmark sources, and verifies production coverage import. PR APIs can omit unchanged files, so their absence is checked against submitted project metadata rather than treated as an analysis exclusion. See the scope investigation.

The quick profile is intended for a smoke test and takes a few minutes:

BENCHMARK_PROFILE=quick .bin/slimfaas-local-benchmark.sh

On Windows, run the script in Git Bash with Python 3.10+. The launcher places the runtime and its descendants in an owned Windows Job Object before execution. Normal completion and an abrupt launcher exit both close the entire process tree. Occupied benchmark ports are rejected before starting or cleaning state. Run python .bin/test-local-benchmark-host.py to verify those lifecycle checks.

Fresh Windows WALs use recorded 64 KiB data chunks; existing unmarked volumes keep their original geometry. Preserve wal/slimdata-chunk-size with the WAL. The Windows investigation retains the failed controls, reproduction commands and validation of large messages, Streams and recovery. This changes neither the load nor its request deadlines.

Run the three-node recovery scenario

The restart-under-load scenario starts the same three-node SlimFaas Local cluster, writes continuously to SlimData, generates application HTTP traffic, kills a non-leader node, and fails unless the leader remains stable while the restarted node reports both /health and /ready successfully and committed Raft entries continue to advance:

RECOVERY_TIMEOUT_SECONDS=180 .bin/slimfaas-local-recovery-benchmark.sh

Use RECOVERY_SKIP_BUILD=true for repeated runs with existing Release binaries and RECOVERY_RUN_ROOT to select the artifact directory. The scenario requires lsof and writes recovery-summary.txt, traffic logs, and the local supervisor log below the selected artifact directory.

The standard profile runs every case three times with longer measurement and warm-up windows:

.bin/slimfaas-local-benchmark.sh

The async-queue profile uses the same payload/concurrency matrix and adds a low-rate paced scenario plus a burst of 1,000 messages at concurrency 64:

BENCHMARK_PROFILE=async-queue \
BENCHMARK_RUN_ROOT=artifacts/slimfaas-local-benchmark/async-baseline \
.bin/slimfaas-local-benchmark.sh

The script builds SlimFaas without the dashboard, builds the benchmark driver, validates benchmarks/slimfaas.local.benchmark.yaml, starts a clean three-node cluster with slimfaas local, runs the matrix, and shuts down every managed process. Docker and Kubernetes are not required.

It requires the repository's .NET 11 SDK plus Bash and curl. Ports 31020-31023, 3162-3164, 31080, and the 32000-32015 process pool must be free.

Results are written below artifacts/slimfaas-local-benchmark/<profile>-<UTC timestamp>/:

  • summary.md: tables for sync overhead, async latency, and scaling milestones;
  • results.json: structured settings and results;
  • latency-samples.csv: one row per measured HTTP request;
  • scaling-timeline.csv: observed replicas and queue depths over time;
  • benchmark-manifest.txt: commit, dirty-worktree flag, SDK, host, and matrix;
  • slimfaas-local.log: control-plane and managed-process output.

Compare an optimization with its baseline

For release safety checks, add --criteria non-regression to the comparison command below. The default remains optimization. Non-regression evaluates the complete sync, async, paced/burst and scaling evidence without requiring the 20–50% optimization targets. It retains the existing 10% throughput/tail guardrails, 20% CPU/message, 10% RSS and 2x Raft-entries/message limits. A missing measurement or failed reference produces INCONCLUSIVE (exit 2), never a passing result.

Async resource collection waits for a fresh diagnostics sample on every node before sending measured requests. CPU and RSS come from the live process collectors across load and delivery drain. After drain, the collector waits for each node's five-second diagnostics exporter to refresh before reading the final Raft counter. This wait is outside the timed load and the CPU/RSS window; the Raft delta includes background entries within that exporter window. It does not extend the 180-second delivery deadline. Initial, final process and final diagnostics snapshots, including per-node timestamps and counters, are retained in AsyncResources / focused-workload Resources for audit. A missing counter, counter reset or refresh timeout cannot produce passing resource evidence. Process start time and CPU/diagnostics/Raft counters are checked per node at each sample and boundary: progress on another node cannot mask a reset. The focused paced/burst comparisons apply the same +20% CPU/message, +10% RAM and 2x Raft/message limits to the median resources of each shape; their resource deltas are retained in comparison.json and comparison.md.

Earlier subsecond bursts could finish between periodic samples and report zero CPU or Raft work. Keep those observations as INCONCLUSIVE and rerun both revisions with the same corrected driver; do not backfill their missing samples.

macOS, Linux ARM64 and Kubernetes campaigns

Use .bin/run-platform-workload.py for one attributable run and .bin/run-platform-matrix.py for serial reference–candidate–candidate–reference blocks. Publish both revisions before starting measurements; use the same prebuilt benchmark and MemoryLab drivers for both. The full HTTP defaults are async-queue, 64/4096/65536/262144/1048576/2000000/2097152/4194304 bytes, concurrency 1/4/16, 2-second warmup, 10-second measurements and three repetitions. MemoryLab defaults are Set and mixed at concurrency 12/48, 30-second warmup and 120-second load, with all-node reads and independent async SHA-256 receipts. Its safety limits remain 90% throughput, 120% p99 and 115% RSS, with zero errors.

After integrating PR #504 and PR #514, build the candidate and comparison reference with SDK 11.0.100 and the same compilation mode. The .NET 11 reference is PR #514's f36084643a75d803051a6918d2950d1a4f674ada, before the collection and reliability changes. Keep the original 496e8739 .NET 10 reference and its observations as historical evidence; do not combine their performance samples with the .NET 11 comparison. Record both source SHAs and the common driver's hash in each new campaign configuration. Existing campaign directories and original persisted volumes must remain available after this toolchain change.

For example, save an environment configuration outside the source tree:

{
  "environment": "macos",
  "before": "/absolute/path/baseline/SlimFaas",
  "after": "/absolute/path/candidate/SlimFaas",
  "before_commit": "<reference-source-SHA>",
  "after_commit": "<candidate-source-SHA>",
  "benchmark": "/absolute/path/SlimFaas.Benchmarks.dll",
  "memorylab": "/absolute/path/SlimFaas.MemoryLab.dll",
  "compare_command": ["dotnet", "/absolute/path/SlimFaas.Benchmarks.dll"]
}

python3 .bin/run-platform-matrix.py --config artifacts/platform-macos.json \
  --output artifacts/platform-macos

The matrix writes every run and all four cross-comparisons. Contradictory guardrails against the two surrounding references trigger one complete ABBA repeat for that block; both attempts remain available. --resume continues an interrupted matrix without overwriting completed or failed evidence. No builds, other measurements or fault campaigns may run concurrently with measurements. Low disk space stops a new phase; preserve state, WALs, snapshots and journals when reclaiming verified inactive build caches or images.

The test-only benchmarks/platform/Dockerfile inherits the exact production runtime image and adds a common load driver, SDK fixtures and Linux fault tools. Build with --build-arg RUNTIME_IMAGE=<source-built-runtime>. Use podman in the matrix configuration, immutable image digests for before/after, and a unique prefix. State is stored on the VM's Linux filesystem, not a macOS bind mount. Podman measures a managed, trimmed ARM64 runtime with the current production Dockerfile; macOS Native AOT results are a separate comparison.

For Kubernetes, use a dedicated four-node kind cluster (one control plane and three workers), an explicit kubeconfig and context kind-slimfaas-pr506. Verify kind's rootless prerequisites, including cgroup v2 delegation. The kind nodes need a VM-native /evidence mount from /var/home/core/slimfaas-pr506. Preload the runtime and common controller images. Set environment to kubernetes, prefix to slimfaas-pr506-<campaign>, and provide kubeconfig, controller_image, before_commit and after_commit. The launcher creates dedicated labelled namespaces, retained persistent volumes, three anti-affined StatefulSet nodes, actual function Deployments and Jobs. Generators and functions run inside the cluster through Services and pod DNS. Port-forwarding is unnecessary for measurements. Campaign namespaces must fit Kubernetes' 63-character limit, including the matrix block, attempt and ordinal suffixes. PersistentVolume names append a storage suffix and can exceed the label-value limit, so volumes carry the campaign ownership label without an app label. Their unique names, claim references and retained storage paths identify each node's data. A launch with unbound claims has no valid workload measurement; preserve its API errors and replay after correcting the deployment with fresh campaign identities. Each matrix phase keeps launcher manifests, ownership records and Kubernetes diagnostics under controller/, alongside its workload reports. The launcher requires this controller directory to be new; existing phase metadata must not be used as the controller output or overwritten during a resume.

Before exporting a Kubernetes phase, stop scales only Deployments and StatefulSets carrying that campaign's label. It then waits up to 180 seconds for their pods to disappear and for other labelled pod writers to finish; completed Job pods remain available as evidence. A deletion timestamp alone does not establish that a process has finished its final WAL flush. controller/shutdown.json retains pod UIDs, pending writers and the final quiescence verdict. A failed stop prevents the VM archive and the next phase from starting. This collection deadline is separate from the unchanged 180-second async delivery drain and the leader-change deadline. The reliability workflow also runs for changes to the platform/Kubernetes harnesses and SDK probes, including pull requests without runtime changes.

collect requests timestamped current container logs and the previous instance when a restart is reported. Originals under controller/pod-logs/ retain pod UID, container identity and restart index; the historical flat filenames remain convenience copies. pod-log-coverage.json records retrieval outcomes, hashes and missing generations. A missing prior log cannot establish absence of managed OOM, even when the current process appears healthy. Long-running controllers can call the same collector with previous_only=True after observed restarts to retain older generations before Kubernetes discards them. Log collection failure is recorded so campaign shutdown can still finish and preserve state.

HTTP and MemoryLab fixtures omit the fault-agent sidecar's containerPort declaration for both revisions; its control socket still listens normally. The historical runtime also bound declared sidecar ports, which conflicts with that agent. The separate chaos fixture declares the sidecar port to exercise the corrected listener ownership. Keep this common performance convention when checking reference readiness; retain failed compatibility controls separately.

Linux fault controls also inspect cgroup socket memory and OOM status. RSS guardrails retain their existing definition, while an unplanned runtime/control OOM fails the controlled recovery campaign even if the process restarts. See the Linux socket-memory controls.

Runtime comparisons include the durable Raft append and local read-application barriers described in the architecture. Keep them enabled: an acknowledgment from a volatile replica cannot be counted as equivalent to a persisted quorum copy when comparing performance.

The platform runner preserves every latency sample in latency-samples.csv.gz. The common driver compresses completed case samples between timed cases, using --samples-format csv.gz; ordinary manual runs still default to CSV. Comparison requires matching sample formats. Compression reduces evidence storage without sampling or dropping request observations. VM exports retain complete WALs and samples in raw.tar.gz, with its SHA-256 in raw-archive.json; comparers extract only the smaller reports and logs. The original VM state remains in place. Extract the archive when inspecting the large raw members rather than keeping an additional uncompressed copy.

After the current guest workload and its writers have exited, filesystem discard can return already unallocated Linux blocks to the Mac's sparse VM disk. Record host/VM free space before and after, and complete this housekeeping before the next timed load. It removes no file, image, WAL, snapshot or volume:

podman machine ssh sudo fstrim -v /

Retain the discard log and any interrupted observations. Filesystem discard is separate from deleting a cache or pruning an unused image.

Long rootless campaigns also consume the Linux user's session-key quota. Inspect /proc/key-users and sysctl kernel.keys.maxkeys kernel.keys.maxbytes in the dedicated VM. If OCI startup reports unable to create session key: disk quota exceeded, raise that VM's quota (for example, sudo sysctl -w kernel.keys.maxkeys=20000 kernel.keys.maxbytes=2000000) and retain the original failed attempt. This is unrelated to filesystem capacity.

sysctl -w settings are lost when the VM restarts. To preserve the campaign's validated key quotas and inotify limits across restarts, install a dedicated configuration inside that VM:

podman machine ssh sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/90-slimfaas-pr506-rootless.conf <<'EOF'
kernel.keys.maxkeys = 20000
kernel.keys.maxbytes = 2000000
fs.inotify.max_user_watches = 524288
fs.inotify.max_user_instances = 524288
EOF
podman machine ssh sudo sysctl -p /etc/sysctl.d/90-slimfaas-pr506-rootless.conf

Recheck these values after a host/VM restart before resuming container campaigns. On macOS, prevent idle sleep for the measurement command's lifetime, for example with caffeinate -ims python3 .bin/run-platform-matrix.py --config config.json --output artifacts/matrix. A host suspension interrupts measurement isolation; retain the partial results and start a fresh complete ABBA block.

The normal probe profile runs readiness and liveness checks with a 300-second startup allowance for retained-state recovery. The endurance profile disables liveness replacement while explicitly suspending only the campaign runtime process; pod UID, PID and process start time fence every signal. Per-pod/per-restart receipts and logs are retained before scaling down. See the reliability guide for fault and ledger invariants. The protocol-probe regression reports crash-to-listener time separately from majority recovery after the listener opens; the latter keeps its 15-second deadline. The existing membership announcement can consume 200 seconds before the restarted listener opens when its first peer is silent. Retain that startup time in the report, even when the subsequent majority check succeeds.

Keep these bounds separate in container endurance campaigns: pass --protocol-startup-timeout 300 --recovery-timeout 180 through the Kubernetes launcher to the chaos driver. The startup option applies only to the process restart and HTTP-listener waits in protocol-timeout; its default remains the recovery timeout for compatibility with existing commands. The subsequent ready/write guard stays fixed at 15 seconds, and recovery/confirmed-drain waits remain at 180 seconds. The report records both the selected startup allowance and actual crash-to-listener time. A startup failure remains a retained failed observation and must not be counted as a completed long endurance.

The command rejects reports whose duration, warm-up, repetitions, payloads, concurrency, or scaling settings differ. It writes:

  • comparison.md: human-readable before/after latency, overhead, throughput, async, scaling, and acceptance verdicts;
  • comparison.json: the same comparison as structured data.

The command exits with a non-zero status when the candidate records errors or timeouts, when the median added p50 reduction is below 20% for 64 B–4 KiB or 40% for 256 KiB–2 MiB, or when added p95/p99 or the throughput ratio regresses by more than 10%. Async latency and scaling timings are reported for context; only their errors and timeouts affect the verdict.

With --profile async, the verdict additionally requires no missing, duplicated, failed, or expired message; median reductions of at least 50% for the HTTP-202 p95 and 40% for the function-arrival p95; and at least 40% p50 improvement for 2 MiB. Each case is also guarded against a p99 or throughput regression above 10%. CPU per message may grow by at most 20%, peak memory by 10%, and Raft entries per message may not exceed 2x the baseline. Missing resource fields in an older results.json remain readable and are displayed as unavailable.

The synchronous and scaling sections are still generated by an async comparison to expose collateral changes. Sync microbenchmark guardrails are informational for --profile async; the async p99/throughput/resource rules and all correctness failures determine that profile's verdict. Use the default --profile sync comparison when sync guardrails must be gating.

What is measured

Warm synchronous overhead

The benchmark target is one minimal HTTP/1.1 server. The driver calls that exact process in two ways:

  1. directly at http://127.0.0.1:31080/echo;
  2. through /function/benchmark-latency/echo.

For each payload size and concurrency, the report includes throughput and HTTP p50, p95, p99, and maximum latency. It then subtracts the direct percentile from the SlimFaas percentile in milliseconds and percent. Calling the same process on both paths isolates the warm routing/proxy overhead from application work.

The standard matrix uses:

  • payloads: 64 B, 4 KiB, 256 KiB, and 2 MiB;
  • closed-loop concurrency: 1 and 16;
  • warm-up: 2 seconds;
  • measurement: 10 seconds;
  • repetitions: 3.

The report uses the median percentile across repetitions and the mean throughput. The driver alternates direct/proxy order between cases to reduce systematic CPU frequency and temperature bias.

Asynchronous latency

Each async case reports two different clocks:

  • acceptance latency: client send until SlimFaas returns HTTP 202 after the request has been durably enqueued;
  • arrival latency: client send until the target handler starts, including enqueue, queue wait, dispatch, and request-body transfer.

For both clocks, the report gives the mean (the simple average) and p50/p95/p99. For example, p95 means that 95% of messages were no slower than that value. The mean is the easiest headline number, while p95 and p99 reveal occasional slow messages that an average can hide. The target also records completion latency in results.json. The target and driver are local processes on the same clock, so UTC ticks can be compared without a network clock-synchronization error. The benchmark waits for every accepted message to be observed by the target and for queue metrics to remain at zero before starting another case.

The 2 MiB case is intentionally above SlimFaas' default 1 MiB async body-offload threshold (strictly greater; exactly 1 MiB stays inline). This makes the matrix cover both inline queue payloads and the cluster-file path. Record SlimFaas__AsyncBodyOffloadThresholdBytes when overriding that default; vary it separately from the fresh WAL geometry and keep it identical across comparison brackets. See async body configuration.

The async profile also records throughput, missing and duplicate IDs, errors, expirations, Raft entries per accepted message, process CPU per message, and peak aggregate SlimFaas working set. The paced scenario measures how quickly a nearly idle queue wakes without waiting for the polling fallback. The burst scenario measures coalescing and backpressure under sudden load.

Scaling speed

benchmark-scale starts at zero replicas. The driver sends a burst of 200 async messages at concurrency 32; each target request takes 250 ms and each replica is limited to one concurrent request. The following durations are measured from the first client send:

  • first and last HTTP 202;
  • desired replicas changing from 0 to at least 1;
  • first ready replica;
  • desired replicas reaching 4;
  • all 4 replicas becoming ready;
  • the ready, in-flight, and retry queues returning to zero.

The first delivered /work request makes the benchmark target expose slimfaas_benchmark_scale_pressure 4 for 30 seconds. SlimFaas scrapes it every second and evaluates max_over_time(slimfaas_benchmark_scale_pressure[30s]). This deterministic demand signal exercises metric discovery, scraping, the internal metric store, PromQL evaluation, scale policy application, local process launch, and health readiness. Queue metrics are observed independently to measure backlog and drain time.

Use the RID matching the host. The JIT publication is self-contained and untrimmed; the native publication uses the product's AOT settings. The campaign requires identical dashboard assets in all publications. SkipClientAppBuild skips compilation but can still copy an existing generated wwwroot; remove it from the benchmark publication copies for a backend-only comparison. The campaign never compiles during measurement. It runs variants sequentially, reverses their order on alternate rounds and rotates the third round. Every repetition starts a clean three-node slimfaas local cluster. The unchanged benchmark driver and target use the same JIT runtime for all four variants.

Each round covers direct/synchronous/asynchronous HTTP, paced and burst queue traffic, scale-to-zero/scale-out, sustained sets, mixed set/delete/increment/ hashset/async operations, cross-node file uploads/reads, and a bounded durable Stream burst. Set/hashset/counter state is checked on all three nodes; queue and Stream delivery checks reject missing or duplicate IDs. The Stream burst must reach zero lag and pending deliveries with committed ACKs. Microbenchmarks exercise larger collection populations separately. File payloads default to 256 KiB and can be changed with --file-bytes. The file workload reuses one ID per worker, uploads to one node and drains a read from the next. It measures warm repeated-file access and HTTP success, without byte-by-byte comparison. Unique 2 MiB async bodies exercise offload separately. --dispatch-parallelism defaults to 16 and sets both async dispatch limits on the benchmark function through a generated local overlay. The original manifest stays unchanged. Use 256 explicitly to retain the original high-parallelism stress profile. Sustained 2 MiB traffic exposed quorum interruptions and delivery deadlines at both capacities 256 and 16 on this three-node setup, including the baseline without ZLinq. Retain unsuccessful attempts alongside completed runs; performance medians conditional on successful completion cannot establish reliability.

CPU and sampled peak RSS sum the runtime nodes, excluding the supervisor, functions and load generator. Async and Stream CPU windows include delivery and drain. RSS reflects process working sets, including shared/native pages; it is different from managed allocation per operation. Data resources include driver startup before load, but end before report serialization and state validation. Data operations may issue multiple HTTP requests. Stream throughput includes delivery/drain; its p95 is append acceptance latency.

The summarizer rejects incomplete rounds and correctness failures. It retains every repetition in comparison.json, reports medians plus rate/CPU/RSS/p95 ranges, and includes the unchanged direct-target control. Compressed per-request HTTP samples, per-case resources, validation logs, binary hashes and settings remain in the campaign directory. A noisy direct control or overlapping repetition ranges limits conclusions about small differences; longer runs alone do not remove shared-host variance.

After an interrupted campaign, repeat its exact command with --resume. The runner checks settings and executable/assembly hashes, skips completed variants, and archives incomplete attempts before restarting them with clean state. It waits for ports to become reusable and accepts TCP TIME_WAIT during restart.

If instability prevents a planned repetition from completing, retain its logs and failure counts. An explicit analysis.json can limit repetitions symmetrically before/after within each runtime mode; --resume honors those limits and the summarizer displays the analyzed counts. Interpret the result correctly

  • Subtract percentiles in milliseconds first. A sub-millisecond direct baseline can make a small absolute delta look large as a percentage.
  • Async HTTP 202 is enqueue latency, not execution latency. Use target delivery percentiles for end-to-end dispatch behavior.
  • Native local scaling measures SlimFaas plus operating-system process startup. It deliberately excludes Kubernetes scheduling, admission, image pulls, CNI, and container runtime time. Run the same driver against a Kubernetes deployment when those costs are part of the question.
  • Function status endpoints have short caches. Scaling times are externally observed milestones with that polling resolution, not internal timestamps.
  • Avoid unrelated workloads, power-saving mode, thermal throttling, and debug builds. Keep the same host, SDK, commit, and matrix for before/after comparisons.
  • A single run is exploratory. Use the standard repetitions, compare medians, and retain the raw manifest and samples for a publishable result.

See Native Local Development Mode for the process orchestrator and Autoscaling for the production scaling model.

python3 .bin/test-platform-validation.py

Preserve original data before recovery or logical PV-content loss.

Request journals and orchestration ownership

C# owns request generation, pacing and latency measurement. The unified driver and MemoryLab compile the same percentile interpolation from benchmarks/Common. Python controls process/pod faults and independently reconciles receipts. Shell scripts prepare environments and invoke these tools; they must not introduce another load generator or silently retry application requests.

Use --journal-directory <new-directory> with run or MemoryLab load when individual outcomes matter. Each process creates a unique JSONL file containing its pod UID, writer ID, UTC and monotonic clock, caller ID, target URI, length and SHA-256 when available, response headers/status/version and transport exceptions. Async response headers also retain QueueElementId, linking the caller ID to the accepted queue element before execution and acknowledgment reconciliation. Intents are flushed before entering the HTTP transport. An exception after that point is recorded as unknown; it is not proof of rejection or non-execution. MemoryLab sync/async calls share the caller ID and SHA-256 with the independent function fixture, and record operation completion only after response validation and draining. Sync still sends one application-level request; no retry is added.

JSONL lines are flushed to the OS, without a per-line disk fsync. They survive a process crash when the OS retains the file; they do not prove host power-loss durability. The independent Python function receipts retain their existing fsync. The HTTP pilot journal observes response headers, not successful full-body consumption. It does not observe transparent transport retries or redirects as separate wire exchanges. Reconcile those with server receipts and runtime logs. Journaling is opt-in and adds driver hashing/I/O cost; use the same setting and binary for both sides of a comparison. Original reports are never retrofilled.

The Kubernetes pod-replacement adapter reuses the three-node campaign manifests and executes the C# generator as a Job. It keeps the deleted function process alive during preStop to distinguish stale connection reuse from pod selection. Function headless DNS excludes unready addresses; Raft's separate headless service retains its own membership policy. API observations include pod UIDs/IPs, termination/readiness, EndpointSlices and events. Runtime debug logs retain the actual sent URLs; receipt headers identify the function that served each request.

The default --replacement-mode terminating retains those established connections until the observation window ends. Use --replacement-mode exit for a separate case where deletion also ends the old fixture process. Its identity is checked before SIGINT, and a replacement UID is never signaled by that action. Keep these two failure modes distinct in the report. --function-delay-seconds 0.5 optionally holds function requests in flight; combine it with C16 and a suitable target rate to exercise active connections rather than merely configuring 16 idle slots. The delay applies to POST workload calls, leaving readiness GETs unaffected. Use --function-controller statefulset --replacement-mode exit to exercise a StatefulSet function with a stable ordinal and a replaced UID/IP. The old process must exit before that controller can recreate its ordinal; the adapter rejects the long preStop mode for this case.

For a separate forensic run, --delivery-trace enables Trace logging at admission, dequeue, HTTP transport entry/result, callback command and committed Raft apply boundaries. Join caller journals' QueueElementId to queue element IDs, worker generation/try number, producer generation/sequence, operation request ID and Raft index/term. A transport entry does not prove bytes reached the function. A network exception may become the existing synthetic HTTP 500; the transport trace keeps that outcome distinct from actual response headers. A confirmed callback command is distinct from proof that it matched a still-running attempt. Missing trace lines never prove non-application; preserve WAL/snapshots for replay, especially on followers and restarts that have no local apply context. Trace logging adds I/O cost: keep this diagnostic separate from ordinary performance acceptance.

Routing cases also use the existing resource sampler to read the owned runtime's CPU ticks, RSS, open FDs and socket FDs every five seconds. Live TCP states are matched to that process's socket inodes; TIME_WAIT and interface byte counters belong to the entire pod network namespace, including probes and diagnostics. Keep this scope and sampler overhead identical across comparisons. Each sample includes pod UID and process start identity; a recycled PID is rejected. Sampling never signals a process and does not rehash the executables on every poll.

python3 .bin/run-kubernetes-routing.py \
  --kubeconfig artifacts/pr506/kubernetes/kubeconfig \
  --namespace slimfaas-pr506-routing-service-example \
  --image localhost/slimfaas-pr506:function-pool-467-03 \
  --controller-image localhost/slimfaas-pr506:routing-tools \
  --source-commit 29daa097fd4562c39e4b362646c16ddd5f1cf7c0 \
  --route service --concurrency 1 --before-seconds 60 --after-seconds 420 \
  --output artifacts/pr506/routing/service-example

Build/import the selected images first. The adapter refuses namespace reuse and clusters outside the dedicated four-node kind-slimfaas-pr506 environment. It retains volumes and evidence after stopping its owned workloads. Execution completion is not a convergence/non-regression verdict: reconcile receipts, unknowns, actual five-minute connection age and the separate 15-second routing budget before issuing one. Use --dry-run to inspect the resource manifest.

During routing teardown, the adapter first scales its owned workloads to zero. It then ends only its Python function fixture, checking namespace/campaign labels, image, command, downward-API pod UID and the container PID1 command before SIGINT. This happens after measurement, keeping the long preStop from adding ten minutes to every case. Other processes are never signaled, and the retained-volume/log quiescence check still runs before export.

For async or mixed routing, the C# generator stops admitting work before a separate 180-second read-only receipt drain. The sampler marks that interval as drain. There is no resubmission. Failed HTTP execution receipts remain separate from body corruption and successful duplicates; a later 2xx execution can reconcile an accepted retry. Controlled-fault duplicate counts are retained rather than erased. Normal benchmark receipt checks still reject duplicates by default. The fault comparison must assess attempts and successful executions before issuing a verdict.

The isolated Service connection-lifetime ABBA report records 38,400 reconciled calls and the actual five-minute pool rotation. It distinguishes a still-alive terminating pod from a stopped destination, and keeps this diagnostic separate from capacity and final-source acceptance.

The headless DNS comparison retains its original pre-traffic health failure and the measurements from all four runs. The async ownership report separates the deterministic worker regression from historical duplicate causes that still require real per-ID traces and affected application replays.

The source f2f80124 publication ledger identifies the new Native AOT executables and shared Linux drivers/images. Publication and CI success remain separate from application and endurance acceptance; follow its recorded preflights before using those images.

Detailed Trace can rotate a Kubernetes log within one pod/container generation. A successful kubectl logs call and unchanged restart count therefore do not establish complete history. The collector now rejects a canonical snapshot that omits a previously captured prefix. It keeps that earlier snapshot and reports the gap; a passing receipt reconciliation does not remove it. The in-cluster chaos backend uses the same UID/restart collector as the host, captures current and previous generations, and saves output before successive intentional kills.

For new dedicated kind clusters, merge this patch into the first control-plane node's configuration, retaining the existing evidence mounts and worker layout:

kubeadmConfigPatches:
  - |
    kind: KubeletConfiguration
    containerLogMaxSize: 128Mi

kind applies the first node's KubeletConfiguration to all nodes. Verify the effective configuration before each comparison series and keep it identical for both variants. This run's four-node dedicated cluster was updated while campaigns were stopped, with original configurations retained and the effective limit verified through each node's configz endpoint. Larger retention does not prove absence of other gaps. The original source-f2 async routing case has complete receipts but incomplete detailed leader history; its per-ID trace verdict remains inconclusive and requires a fresh run.
